verses.text: Paul and his companions traveled through Amphipolis and Apollonia and came to Thessalonica, where there was a Jewish synagogue.
As usual, Paul went in and spent three Sabbaths discussing the Scriptures with them.
He explained and showed that the Messiah had to suffer and rise from the dead. “This Jesus I’m telling you about is the Messiah,” he said.
Some of them were convinced and joined Paul and Silas, along with many devout Greeks and quite a few prominent women.

But the Jews who refused to believe gathered some troublemakers from the marketplace, formed a crowd, and stirred up the city. They attacked Jason’s house, trying to bring Paul and Silas out to the crowd.
When they couldn’t find them, they dragged Jason and some other believers before the city officials, shouting, “These people who have turned the whole world upside down have come here too!
“Jason welcomed them into his home. They’re all defying Caesar’s decrees by saying there is another king—Jesus!”
The crowd and city officials were alarmed when they heard this.
They made Jason and the others post bail, then let them go.
That night the believers sent Paul and Silas to Berea. When they arrived, they went into the Jewish synagogue.
The people there were more open-minded than those in Thessalonica. They eagerly received the message and examined the Scriptures every day to see if it was true.
Many of them believed, including a number of prominent Greek women and men.
But when the Jews in Thessalonica learned that Paul was announcing God’s word in Berea too, they came there and stirred up the crowds.
The believers immediately sent Paul toward the coast, while Silas and Timothy stayed behind.
Those escorting Paul took him as far as Athens. Then they returned with instructions for Silas and Timothy to join him as soon as possible.
While Paul waited for them in Athens, he was deeply troubled to see that the city was full of idols.
He reasoned in the synagogue with Jews and devout Gentiles, and every day in the marketplace with anyone who happened to be there.

Some Epicurean and Stoic philosophers argued with him. Some asked, “What is this talker trying to say?” Others said, “He seems to be promoting foreign gods,” because Paul was announcing Jesus and the resurrection.
They took him to the Areopagus and said, “Can we hear more about this new teaching you’re sharing?
“You’re saying some strange things, and we want to know what they mean.”
All the Athenians and the foreigners living there spent their time talking about or listening to the latest ideas.
Paul stood in the middle of the Areopagus and said, “People of Athens, I can see that you are very religious in every way.
“As I walked around and looked at the things you worship, I even found an altar with this inscription: ‘TO AN UNKNOWN GOD.’ What you worship without knowing, I’m now announcing to you.
“The God who made the world and everything in it is Lord of heaven and earth. He doesn’t live in temples built by human hands.
“He isn’t served by human hands as if he needed anything. He gives everyone life, breath, and everything else.
“From one ancestor he made every nation of people to live across the whole earth. He set their appointed times and the boundaries of where they would live.
“He did this so they might seek God and perhaps reach out for him and find him—though he is never far from any of us.
“For in him we live, move, and exist. As some of your own poets have said, ‘We are also his children.’
“Since we are God’s children, we shouldn’t imagine that God’s nature is like gold, silver, or stone carved by human skill and imagination.
“God overlooked the times when people didn’t know better, but now he commands everyone everywhere to turn back to him.
“He has set a day when he will judge the world fairly through the man he appointed. God has given everyone proof of this by raising him from the dead.”
When they heard about resurrection from the dead, some mocked Paul. Others said, “We want to hear more about this another time.”
Then Paul left the gathering.
But some people joined him and believed. Among them were Dionysius, a member of the Areopagus, a woman named Damaris, and others.
